title: Multipolarity Has Failed
author: Thomas Fazi
content:
![Multipolarity Has
Failed](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-28-at-7.07.32
---AM.png)

It is now conventional wisdom that the United States is lurching from one
blunder to the next. By antagonizing Russia and China simultaneously, it
pushed them into each other's arms; by weaponizing the dollar and slapping
tariffs on friend and foe alike, it has accelerated de-dollarization. In Iran,
meanwhile, the US has failed to achieve regime change while sustaining massive
damage to its bases in the Middle East. Finally, there is broad agreement that
Ukraine--and by extension NATO--is losing its war with Russia, dealing yet
another devastating blow to American power. America's terminal decline, it is
widely assumed, will force Washington to accept a diminished role and
accommodate a new, multipolar world order.

I have made this argument myself more than once. But lately, I have started to
wonder whether those of us who welcome the rise of a new multipolar order have
allowed our wishes to get ahead of reality. The evidence of the past year
points in a different direction, nowhere more clearly than in the growing
paralysis of BRICS, the organization of emerging economies that has positioned
itself as a counterweight to US dominance.

It is necessary to distinguish here between relative weight and relative
power. In terms of weight--especially economic weight--multipolarity is
already a reality. The US economy accounts for a much smaller share of the
global economy than it did a decade ago, thanks above all to China's rise. But
has this decline in relative weight been matched by a comparable decline in
power? Not really.
